items.title: Closed-Loop Reinforcement Learning in De Novo Molecular Design: Bridging Generative AI with Automated Chemical Synthesis
items.abstract: Closed-loop reinforcement learning offers a promising approach to integrating generative molecular design with automated chemical synthesis and experimental evaluation. However, translating autonomous chemical optimization into pharmaceutical discovery remains challenging because biological measurements are often delayed, variable, and affected by assay limitations. This critical review and perspective examines current autonomous discovery platforms and evaluates the challenges associated with incorporating physical experimental feedback into molecular optimization. It proposes an uncertainty-aware, multi-objective reward architecture and a four-gate qualification framework covering operational synthesizability, analytical identity and purity, biological assay validity, and governed policy updating. Particular attention is given to distinguishing statistically censored measurements from pharmacologically confounded or invalid observations. The article also introduces supervised autonomy as a practical governance approach in which automated systems perform routine experimental operations while scientific experts retain responsibility for critical decisions. The proposed framework provides a foundation for improving the reliability, interpretability, and practical implementation of experimentally informed molecular discovery. Prospective validation remains necessary to establish its effectiveness.

items.title: Cognitive Conflict and Critical Thinking Skills in Science Education: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Critical thinking is an essential competency in science education because it enables students to analyze information, evaluate evidence, draw inferences, and make reasoned decisions. Cognitive conflict—arising when students’ prior conceptions encounter information or phenomena inconsistent with their existing understanding—may provide opportunities to reconsider explanations and examine evidence. This review examines (1) how cognitive conflict strategies have been designed and implemented to support critical thinking in science education, (2) how critical thinking has been operationalized and assessed, and (3) opportunities and challenges associated with integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and adaptive learning. The study uses a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) with narrative synthesis. Sixteen articles were mapped for the period October 10, 2016–October 10, 2026. The mapped literature includes studies on cognitive conflict in physics education, instructional media development, critical thinking assessment, conceptual change, and GenAI use. The preliminary synthesis indicates that cognitive conflict has been integrated into inquiry learning, discovery learning, interactive multimedia, e-books, augmented reality, and educational websites. However, only a small subset of the mapped studies directly measured critical thinking, while others focused on conceptual understanding, misconception remediation, scientific literacy, creativity, or product development. The GenAI literature provides contextual insights into personalization and the risk of reduced cognitive engagement, but does not establish the effectiveness of integrating GenAI with cognitive conflict in physics education. The review identifies a need to align cognitive conflict activities with measurable critical thinking indicators and to evaluate GenAI as a scaffold.

items.abstract: This book develops a unified governance framework for systems that retrieve, generate, infer, remember and act on information from large language models and retrieval augmented pipelines to autonomous multi agent systems. Eleven chapters and eight appendices integrate three disciplinary lenses-technology, law and economics-across the full lifecycle: data quality, lineage and provenance; global data protection law and intellectual property; the economics of data governance; digital trust, cybersecurity and zero-trust architecture; ethics and responsible AI; governing generative AI pipelines; governing agentic AI and multi-agent systems; data governance in elections and the public sphere; AI regulation across six jurisdictions; and the design of a governance control plane for 2030. Each chapter is anchored in Indian law and institutions while maintaining a comparative, cross jurisdictional perspective.

items.title: Developers as Managers of AI Agents: A Workplace Shadowing Study
items.abstract: As AI coding agents become more autonomous, developers increasingly direct, coordinate, and check their work. Yet little is known about these practices in everyday professional development. We shadowed 11 professional developers across approximately 15 hours of work, coded their activities and task transitions, analyzed 255 submitted prompts, and conducted 4.6 hours of follow-up interviews. Developers spent an average of 33.4% of observed time formulating prompts or checking AI responses, with task-switching rates ranging from 0 to 101.6 switches per hour. Beyond producing artifacts, prompts supported understanding, requirements clarification, agent configuration, and coordination. We identified three recurring patterns: \textit{Supervisor}, involving direct artifact inspection; \textit{Delegator}, involving dialogue-based coordination and delegated implementation and checking; and \textit{Learner}, involving agents primarily to build understanding. Developers sought technical information from agents and organizational context, authority, and alignment from colleagues. Our findings suggest future studies of how developers manage attention across concurrent agent tasks and tools that support verification, coordination, and learning.

items.title: Digital Constitutionalism and the Protection of Fundamental Rights in the Age of AI: Rethinking Privacy, Equality and Freedom of Expression
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) now decides who receives police protection and who gets government benefits and who gets employment or credit approval and who gets their online content promoted or deleted. The academic research and legal regulations that follow treat the resulting privacy violations and the breaks of equality and the restrictions on free speech as different issues. The paper presents three interrelated elements which demonstrate their relationship through three specific aspects: surveillance and profiling drive people to stop talking then automated content control systems create unfair distribution of when users speak and finally data practices which privacy legislation aims to control lead to unfair scoring outcomes. The study employs doctrinal and comparative approaches to examine three questions: (1) Do Articles 14, 19(1)(a) and 21 of the Indian Constitution provide sufficient protection against AI-related harms (2) What are the strengths and weaknesses of European Union and United States regulations governing AI systems used by public and private organizations (3) What protective measures should India implement. The Indian constitutional doctrine demonstrates strong power but the Indian legal system fails to provide sufficient support for automated decision-making and State exemptions and private-sector discrimination and remedies. The system establishes a comprehensive framework that consists of four hierarchical levels which include constitutional and legislative and institutional and remedial components. The law is stated as at 19 October 2026.

items.title: Digital-Based Career Counseling in the Era of Revolusi Industri 4.0 : Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: The Industrial Revolution 4.0 has significantly transformed various aspects of human life, particularly in education and employment, through the integration of digital technology, artificial intelligence, big data, and the Internet of Things. These rapid changes demand new competencies such as digital literacy, critical thinking, adaptability, and career flexibility. In response to these challenges, digital-based career counseling has emerged as a strategic innovation to support students’ career development and readiness for the modern workplace. This study employs a literature review approach by analyzing recent national and international scientific publications indexed in Sinta, Scopus, and Google Scholar within the last five years. The analysis focuses on key themes including theoretical foundations, implementation models, benefits, and challenges of digital career counseling. The findings indicate that integrating classical career theories, such as Holland’s RIASEC personality typology and Super’s life-span, life-space theory, with digital platforms enhances accessibility, efficiency, and personalization of counseling services. Digital tools such as video conferencing, learning management systems, online assessments, and social media platforms contribute to improving career adaptability, career optimism, and employability skills among students. However, challenges remain in terms of counselors’ digital competence, ethical considerations, data security, and maintaining emotional connection in virtual interactions. Therefore, successful implementation of digital-based career counseling requires collaboration among government institutions, educational organizations, and technology developers to ensure effective, ethical, and student-centered services in the era of the Industrial Revolution 4.0.

items.title: Does Agentic AI Thin Out Entry-Level Employment? A Pre-Registered Test Using the Age Structure of U.S. Occupations, 2019–2026
items.abstract: This registration fixes, before the relevant outcome data are accessed, the hypotheses, data, variables, models and decision rules for a test of whether agentic AI systems accelerate the decline of early-career employment inside AI-exposed U.S. occupations. Between 2019 and 2024, occupations more exposed to large language models saw a larger fall in the share of workers aged 20–34, while their total employment did not fall (Thalassinidis & Bowen, The Price of Judgment, in preparation). Agentic systems, which carry out multi-step workflows and shift human work toward oversight and verification, may speed up this pattern. Using annual American Community Survey microdata (2019 and 2021–2026, with a pre-specified update for 2027), the primary test asks whether the relationship between occupational AI exposure and the early-career share bends more steeply after 2024 than its 2019–2024 trend, in a state-by-occupation panel. Secondary tests compare the agentic period with the generative-AI years alone (2022–2024), and examine whether any acceleration is larger in lower-consequence occupations and where agentic AI use is observed in API traffic. We also test that total employment is not affected. Only the 2019 and 2024 ACS data had been accessed at registration. The full plan, power simulation and data-access statement are attached. A companion preprint is posted on EdArXiv: https://osf.io/preprints/edarxiv/4a3vc_v1 (pending moderation at the time of registration).

items.title: EFFICIENT USE OF ECONOMIC RESOURCES IN THE CONTEXT OF DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION
items.abstract: This article examines the theoretical and methodological foundations of the efficient use of economic resources in the context of digital transformation, with particular emphasis on the impact of digital technologies on production processes, labor productivity, capital utilization, and management efficiency. The study also analyzes the role of data-driven management, artificial intelligence, cloud computing, automation, and digital platforms in improving the allocation and utilization of economic resources. In addition, the implications of digitalization for economic efficiency are considered, including technological investment, human capital development, information security, and organizational transformation. Based on the analysis, scientific and practical recommendations are developed to enhance the efficiency of economic resource utilization under conditions of digital transformation.

items.title: Explainable AI for Fraud Alert Review in Community Banks and Credit Unions: A Narrative Review of Architectures, Analyst Workflows, and Governance
items.abstract: Community banks and credit unions face the same fraud schemes as large banks, but with far fewer analysts and data scientists. Machine-learning detectors help, yet an alert that gives no reason leaves the analyst to reconstruct the logic by hand, which slows investigations and complicates regulatory examinations. This narrative review looks at how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is being applied to fraud alerts in small financial institutions. Drawing on six recent sources, we trace the shift from rule-based systems to machine learning, describe architectural patterns that place an explanation layer between a detection model and the analyst, and discuss how explanations may shorten investigations, support analyst feedback, and strengthen model governance. One study reports that pairing ensemble anomaly detection with XAI reduced average analysis time from 4.2 hours to 35 minutes; we treat this as a single, unreplicated result. The evidence base is small, relies on single studies, and includes working papers and journals of uneven rigor, and it offers no shared benchmarks or analyst-centred evaluations. We close with practical implications for small institutions and open questions for future research.

items.title: Exploring clinician interpretability of AI decision support systems for surgical anatomy recognition
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) decision support systems for surgery hold promise but face barriers to adoption, particularly around the interpretability of their outputs. We conducted an international cross-sectional survey of 47 neurosurgeons to evaluate perspectives on literature-derived explanatory techniques for AI-generated anatomical segmentations, using endoscopic pituitary surgery as a high-risk exemplar. Participants ranked certainty scores, certainty maps, saliency maps, scene similarity scores, and nearest-neighbour illustrations, and rated them using a modified Explanation Satisfaction Scale alongside free-text feedback. Certainty-based techniques were consistently ranked and rated highest - valued for aligning with surgical decision-making by conveying confidence (via scores) and anatomical boundaries (via maps). Saliency- and similarity-based methods were judged less clinically relevant and better suited to educational settings. Therefore, certainty-based techniques appear most acceptable to surgeons for improving the interpretability of AI-assisted anatomical navigation systems, though their impact on trust calibration and performance requires prospective evaluation across surgical domains.

items.title: Exploring the Role of AI in Hybrid Work Within Software Engineering
items.abstract: Abstract This paper reports insights from the 4th International Workshop on Global and Hybrid Work in Software Engineering (GoHyb 2026), in which workshop participants, including Agile researchers and practitioners, explored positive and negative future scenarios of AI-supported hybrid and remote work. Our analysis of the discussion shows that participants viewed AI as especially consequential for hybrid work because it can support task review, synthesis, summarization, and asynchronous coordination across distributed teams. At the same time, they expressed concerns that increased AI mediation may weaken human communication, reduce critical discussion, and undermine psychological safety and social connection. Overall, the findings suggest that the central challenge is not simply adopting AI tools, but shaping human–AI collaboration in ways that strengthen coordination without endangering the human capabilities on which software teams rely. The paper closes with implications for future research on AI-enabled hybrid work in software engineering.

items.title: Faculty and administrative perspectives on artificial intelligence tool integration in higher education using cultural historical activity theory
items.abstract: This study explores faculty and administrative perspectives on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education at Zayed University–Abu Dhabi, within the College of Technological Innovation. Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) is used as an interpretive lens to examine how faculty perceive both the opportunities and challenges associated with AI tool integration, particularly in relation to student engagement and learning. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with faculty members and senior administrative staff to explore perceived benefits, risks, and institutional expectations surrounding AI use. Participants perceived AI as having the potential to support personalized learning and reduce administrative workload, while also raising concerns regarding ethics, assessment integrity, digital dependence, and uncertainty surrounding institutional policy. Several systemic tensions emerged across CHAT components, reflecting misalignments between tools, rules, roles, and expectations in AI-supported teaching. The study highlights the need for clear regulatory frameworks, professional development, and ongoing dialogue to guide ethical and pedagogically grounded AI adoption. These findings contribute to current discussions on how faculty and administrators perceive AI integration in higher education and the conditions required to support responsible and educationally meaningful implementation. This study examines faculty and administrator perceptions and does not directly measure student engagement or learning outcomes. Clinical trial: Not applicable.

items.title: From AI Assistants to AI-Dev-Systems: A Three-Layer Model for Human-AI Collaboration in Agile Software Development
items.abstract: Abstract Context: For decades, integrating new capabilities into agile teams, whether UX practices or emerging technologies, has followed a consistent paradigm: teams remain stable while methods adapt. Applied to AI, this approach produces fragmented tooling, governance uncertainty, and vibe coding : unstructured AI use that prevents cumulative organizational capability. We argue this integration paradigm, successful for disciplines like UX, may be inadequate for AI’s transformative scope. Objective: We reframe AI integration as an organizational design problem: how should teams restructure around AI-Dev-Systems , configured environments of AI agents, workflows, and knowledge bases functioning as shared infrastructure? Method: We propose a three-layer model extending platform engineering: (1) System Teams design AI-Dev-Systems; (2) Platform Teams maintain them; (3) Product Teams develop software within them. Results: Developers shift from producers to stewards monitoring AI outputs. Iteration cycles compress, paradoxically elevating product thinking: when implementation ceases to be the bottleneck, what to build matters more than how . XP practices persist but transform into governance mechanisms for AI-generated work. Conclusion: Teams should restructure around AI-Dev-Systems rather than adopt AI tools, our three-layer model offers a structured provocation to reframe the discourse.

items.title: From Intelligence to Autonomy: Foundations and Construction of Autonomous Agents for Future Intelligent Systems
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is moving from one-off perception and generation tasks toward long-term planning, tool use, and interaction with real environments. Greater task competence, however, does not automatically yield autonomy: an external actor may still have to set goals, sustain operating conditions, detect failures, and approve updates. We define an autonomous agent as a system that, within explicit identity and authority boundaries, maintains both task goals and viability conditions, acts continuously using models of the world and itself, and adjusts its control mechanisms and long-term capabilities through feedback. We trace the conceptual path from homeostasis and feedback control to autopoiesis and biological autonomy. We then distinguish six lines of operationalization: computational autopoiesis, behavior-based robotics, agent formalization, adaptive software, embodied adaptation, and robotic self-modeling. On this basis, we propose a one-boundary, four-loop framework in which Operational, Viability, Reflexive, and Learning loops organize task execution, self-maintenance, metacontrol, and governed learning. Five paired simulation experiments test permission constraints, road-closure response, health maintenance, capability re-estimation, and cross-task learning. Their results provide preliminary evidence for the feasibility of these mechanisms, while broader environments and physical systems remain to be tested.

items.title: From Mobile Learning to Artificial Intelligence: Evolving UTAUT Constructs in Educational Technology Adoption
items.abstract: The Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) has played a crucial role in understanding technology adoption in education. This study examines the evolution of UTAUT constructs over three technological periods: the early adoption period (2003 to 2010), the mobile and social media Boom (2011 to 2016), and the artificial intelligence and digital transformation era (2017 to present). Using a one-stage meta-analytic structural equation modelling (OSMASEM) approach, data from 73 studies were analysed to evaluate relationships among key constructs, including performance expectancy (PE), effort expectancy (EE), social influence (SI), facilitating conditions (FC), behavioural intention (BI), and use behaviour (UB). The findings revealed substantial variability across contexts and constructs, with BI consistently emerging as the strongest predictor of UB, underscoring its centrality in technology adoption. The influence of PE on BI increased over time, reflecting technological advancements that improved performance outcomes. The importance of FC in predicting UB also grew, emphasising the role of infrastructure and technical support in adoption. These insights highlight the dynamic nature of UTAUT constructs, providing actionable recommendations for educators, policymakers, and technology developers to align strategies with evolving user needs and expectations in educational contexts. This study reinforces UTAUT’s relevance in addressing contemporary technological challenges.

items.title: Generative AI in Values Education: Affordances, Ethical Risks and Implications for Teaching
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has become ordinary in university study, and students increasingly bring to it the questions about right and wrong that they once brought to teachers. Institutional guidance still treats GenAI mainly as a threat to academic integrity, leaving unsettled what kind of moral participant a language model can be. This article offers a theoretical account of that question. It characterises values education as a relational practice and specifies three conditions that any occupant of the educator's position must satisfy: answerability, exemplarity and address. It then distinguishes five affordances of GenAI, namely the generation of moral content, the simulation of perspectives, Socratic questioning, feedback on moral reasoning, and a tacit curriculum of machine authority, and analyses the risk internal to each. These risks fall into epistemic, relational, axiological and agentic families and are connected rather than independent. The central argument is that a generative model can be a moral interlocutor but not a values educator: it cannot be answerable for what it says, cannot exemplify a life, and cannot address a particular student. Four implications for teaching and institutional design follow.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence in research protocol review: a scoping review
items.abstract: This registration documents a scoping review examining the applications of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), particularly large language models, in the scientific, methodological, and ethical review of research protocols and related research documents. The objective is to map published evidence on the use of GenAI in research protocol assessment and identify knowledge gaps concerning accuracy, reproducibility, algorithmic bias, human oversight, data security, and institutional feasibility. The review follows the methodological guidance of the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Eligibility criteria are organized using the Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework and encompass research protocols, scientific proposals, and related documents evaluated using generative AI in clinical, academic, scientific, and institutional settings. Literature searches were reported in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science Core Collection through October 22, 2026. The documented study-selection flow comprises 261 identified records, 161 full-text documents assessed, and 10 publications included in the synthesis. The evidence is synthesized descriptively across document extraction, methodological and ethical inconsistency detection, rubric-based assessment, research proposal prioritization, and support for ethics review. The review also examines limitations relevant to implementation in healthcare research institutions. This registration is being created after the literature search, screening, and evidence synthesis were conducted. It therefore constitutes a retrospective documentation of the research process rather than a prospective preregistration. Supporting methodological materials and reproducibility records will be associated with the registration as available.

items.abstract: Employees regularly shift between messages, meetings, complex assignments, and urgent requests, yet the psychological significance of these transitions remains difficult to isolate from general workload. This cross-sectional study examines reported multitasking demands, perceived work-related stress, anxiety symptoms, and work organisation/control using 200 records and a researcher-developed 28-item questionnaire. Four planned Pearson correlations, internal-consistency assessments, and exploratory adjusted regressions were evaluated, with confidence intervals, Holm correction, and sensitivity checks. Multitasking was correlated with stress (r = .604, 95% CI [.508, .685]) and anxiety (r = .564, 95% CI [.461, .652]). Stress and anxiety were closely associated (r = .836, 95% CI [.789, .874]). The negative correlation between work organisation/control and stress was not statistically significant (r = −.100, p = .158). Scale reliability estimates ranged from .795 to .889. These results are correlational rather than causal; the anxiety and stress measures also have potential conceptual overlap. The dataset was supplied as collected survey responses, but its substantial overlap with an earlier demonstration dataset warrants independent provenance review before treating numerical results as authenticated empirical evidence. The study highlights priorities for better instrument validation, work-design research, and longitudinal replication.

items.title: Human Versus AI Feedback for Aligning Large Language Models: A Comparative Review of RLHF and RLAIF
items.abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences commonly relies on reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), which depends on costly preference labels collected from human annotators. Reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) replaces some or all of these labels with judgments produced by an LLM. This paper presents a focused comparative review of RLHF and RLAIF based on twelve core publications. We describe the standard RLHF pipeline, organize related AI-feedback methods (Constitutional AI, RLAIF, direct RLAIF, direct preference optimization, self-rewarding models, and generative reward models) in a common taxonomy, and compile the empirical evidence reported in the literature on performance, cost, and the reliability of AI evaluators. In one controlled study, RLAIF matched RLHF on summarization and helpful dialogue and exceeded it on harmless dialogue, whereas other work indicates that the gains from AI feedback depend About the base model, the critic, and how they connect teacher and critic models. Studies of LLM judges further report high agreement with humans alongside position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases. We conclude that the available evidence supports RLAIF as a way to reduce, but not eliminate, the need for human feedback, and we identify the scarcity of direct head-to-head comparisons as the main open gap. No new experiments were conducted.

items.title: Human–AI Collaboration for Scaling Agile Regression Testing: An Agentic-AI Teammate from Manual to Automated Testing
items.abstract: Abstract Automated regression testing is essential for maintaining rapid, high-quality delivery in Agile and Scrum organizations. Many teams, including Hacon (a Siemens company), face a persistent gap: validated test specifications accumulate faster than they are automated, limiting regression coverage and increasing manual work. This paper reports an exploratory industrial case study of the Hacon Test Automation Copilot, an agentic AI system that generates system-level regression test scripts from validated specifications using retrieval-augmented generation and a multi-agent workflow. Integrated with Hacon’s CI pipelines, the Copilot operates asynchronously as a “silent AI teammate”, producing candidate scripts for human review. Mixed-method evaluation shows the AI accelerates script authoring and increases throughput, with 30–50% code reuse. However, human review remains necessary for maintainability and correct domain interpretation. Clear specifications, explicit governance, and ongoing human–AI collaboration are critical. We conclude with lessons for scaling regression automation and enabling effective human–AI teaming in Agile settings.

items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Employee Productivity and Managerial Decision-Making
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology influencing employee productivity and managerial decision-making in contemporary organisations. This study examines the impact of AI adoption on workplace efficiency, employee performance, and the quality of managerial decisions. AI-powered tools facilitate task automation, data analysis, workflow optimisation, and real-time information processing, enabling employees to improve productivity and managers to make faster, evidence-based decisions. However, the effectiveness of AI depends on factors such as technological infrastructure, employee competencies, organisational readiness, and ethical implementation. The study also considers potential challenges, including job displacement, algorithmic bias, data privacy concerns, and excessive dependence on automated systems. It emphasises the importance of human–AI collaboration in achieving sustainable organisational performance. The findings are expected to provide insights into how organisations can strategically integrate AI into business operations while maintaining accountability, employee engagement, and managerial effectiveness. The study contributes to understanding AI-driven workplace transformation and its implications for organisational growth and competitiveness

items.title: Individual's Trust in AI Agents: A Meta-Analysis of Empirical Evidence
items.abstract: This meta-analysis synthesizes empirical evidence on individuals' trust in AI agents. Three research questions guide the synthesis: (RQ1) which human, agent, and contextual factors predict trust in AI agents; (RQ2) how trust relates to reliance behavior, acceptance and intention to use, and task performance; and (RQ3) how agent type, task risk, trust-measure type, study design, and publication era moderate these relationships. Eligible studies are quantitative, peer-reviewed journal articles and full conference papers (2016 to present) that measure trust toward an interactive agent itself; purely physical robots, non-interactive recommenders, and preprints without a published version are excluded. Effect sizes will be pooled as correlations (r) using three-level random-effects models, following PRISMA 2020 reporting standards.

items.title: Introducing Agile Team Practices in Capstone Courses: Impact on Student Collaboration
items.abstract: Abstract Software engineering capstone courses provide students with real-world team project experience, but active and even collaboration within teams remains hard to achieve. In this experience report, we describe how incorporating activities into the assessment structure of a large undergraduate capstone course changed students’ teamwork experiences. In 2024, agile practices, such as pair programming, daily stand-up meetings, and collaborative planning sessions, were integrated into the grading system, partly to address collaboration issues and partly to respond to increased use of Generative AI tools like ChatGPT. We analyzed data from 872 student surveys across four course offerings from 2022 to 2025, together with 12 semi-structured interviews. Across surveys and interviews, students reported that the agile practices were associated with greater accountability, reflection, and participation, and made collaboration more visible and harder to postpone. In 2025, 74% of students described AI strictly as a tool rather than a team member, with AI use concentrated in debugging, concept explanation, and design discussion. We discuss implications for collaboration-focused assessment in capstone courses in the context of growing AI use, and provide an overview of the team activities as an operational template for educators.

items.title: Is our future ready for the future? Investigating speech and language therapy students’ literacy and awareness of artificial intelligence: a descriptive and correlational study
items.abstract: Although AI awareness is increasing in health and education, research specifically focused on Speech-Language Therapy (SLT) remains limited. This study investigated the knowledge, awareness, and literacy levels of SLT students regarding AI, examining the influence of academic year and prior coursework on these variables. A total of 412 undergraduate SLT students (M age = 21.5, SD = 3.43; 366 F, 45 M) from various universities in Türkiye participated. Data were collected via the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale and the Artificial Intelligence Awareness Survey. Analysis included descriptive statistics, Kruskal-Wallis tests for grade-level comparisons, and Mann-Whitney U tests for prior AI exposure. Spearman correlation and Chi-square tests examined relationships between subscales and categorical variables. Participants demonstrated high overall AI literacy scores, with no significant differences across grade levels. Strong positive correlations were observed among all subscales of the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, particularly between “Use” and “Evaluation” (ρ = .702, p < .001), indicating that higher usage levels relate to better output assessment. Conversely, a weak correlation between “Ethics” and “Use” ( ρ = .225, p < .001) suggested that technical proficiency does not necessarily correspond with ethical awareness. In the awareness survey, a notable proportion of participants remained neutral on several items; however, over 70% expressed excitement about AI advancements and agreed that AI would enhance their professional skills. SLT students generally possess a considerable level of AI literacy but exhibit caution and uncertainty regarding its clinical integration. This hesitancy suggests that students perceive their current knowledge as insufficient for practical application. The findings underscore the need to integrate structured AI curricula into SLT education, with a focus on professional and ethical dimensions. Notably, senior students expressed stronger concerns about AI's potential impact on future demand for SLT services, highlighting the importance of fostering AI literacy and addressing career-related apprehensions to better prepare students for future clinical practice.

items.title: Large Language Model Soundness: A Survey of Knowledge Grounding, Trust Assessment, and Behavioral Control
items.abstract: Deliverable D4.1 (WP4 midterm state-of-the-art report) of the ARMADA MSCA Doctoral Network, funded by Horizon Europe under Grant Agreement No. 101168951 and by the Swiss State Secretariat for Education, Research and Innovation (SERI) under contract No 25.00154. Large language models now mediate search, programming, decision support, and scientific work, but fluent output is not necessarily trustworthy. We call a system sound when its behavior is reliable under immaterial variation, its claims are supported by appropriate evidence, and its confidence reflects the likelihood that those claims are correct. We survey work from 2021 to 2026, with earlier foundational results, and organize it around three questions. Reliable Knowledge Grounding asks whether an answer rests on the right evidence and uses that evidence faithfully, covering retrieval decisions, knowledge conflicts, and contextual hallucination. Verification, Robustness, and Confidence asks when an answer deserves trust, covering methods for checking answers, testing their stability, quantifying uncertainty, and identifying alignment-induced overconfidence. Post-Training and Inference-Time Control asks how sound behavior can be induced and enforced through post-training and controlled during generation. We judge each method by what it contributes to soundness. We then ask how those methods transfer to high-stakes domains, other languages, and multimodal evidence, and how the same checks apply when models plan and call tools over long horizons.

items.abstract: This paper presents Zea, a prototype Meta-Cognitive AI Architecture, and reports an empirical behavioral evaluation conducted through black-box testing. The architecture integrates operational monitoring, memory, identity representation, self-reflection, ethical evaluation, empathy, creativity, decision-making, communication, and adaptive development. Its design is organized around a central Zea Core and a Meta-Cognitive Supervisory Layer. The empirical evaluation is based on 69 recorded human–AI interaction tests (T-001–T-069). The study examines observable response patterns, self-referential and metacognitive behavior, safety-oriented responses, and documented anomalies through black-box observation. The findings describe the prototype's observable behavior under the tested conditions. They do not establish phenomenal consciousness or subjective experience. items.title: Nursing Students' Awareness, Perceptions, and Attitudes Toward Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: A Cross-Sectional Study in Erbil, Iraq
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence is increasingly influencing healthcare delivery and nursing education. Understanding nursing students' perceptions is important for preparing future professionals to use AI responsibly. Objective: To assess nursing students' awareness, experiences, perceptions, and training needs concerning artificial intelligence in healthcare. Methods: A descriptive, survey-based study was conducted among 175 nursing students at Cihan University-Erbil, Iraq. Data were collected using a 22-item closed-ended questionnaire and summarized using descriptive statistics. Results: Most participants were aware of AI (81.7%), and 56.6% reported previous AI use. Approximately 64.6% believed that deep learning-based AI could improve patient care, while 68.0% recognized its potential to facilitate communication across language barriers. Only 30.3% had received formal AI training, and 63.4% believed that additional training was necessary. Concerns included possible reductions in human nursing skills through excessive AI dependence. Conclusion: Nursing students demonstrated substantial awareness of AI and generally positive perceptions of its potential applications. However, limited formal training and concerns about professional skills indicate the need for structured AI education, ethical guidance, and continued human oversight. Further research involving multiple institutions is recommended.

items.title: Of Silicon and Cells: Ethical and Safety Concerns Regarding Artificial Intelligence Usage in the Biomedical Sciences—A Narrative Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), most pointedly through advancements in large language models (LLMs), has dominated the media and has expansive promise in improving productivity in a myriad of fields, notably the life sciences. The expansion of AI into the field has encompassed nearly every domain from research to healthcare and appears to have an inertia that will make it difficult to change the course of its adoption. Given this rapid pace of adoption, it is crucial to reflect on these advancements and their place in the modern life sciences to understand the evolving ethical, medico-legal, and scientific challenges the use of such technology poses for practitioners of the life sciences, specifically, the biomedical sciences. Herein, the authors narratively review the current usage of AI with respect to clinical care, research production and integrity, as well as an epidemiologic purview of technology.

items.title: ORGANIZATIONAL BEHAVIOUR AND WORKPLACE PSYCHOLOGY
items.abstract: Organizational behaviour explains how people interpret, experience, and influence work in conditions shaped by relationships, institutions, technologies, and unequal authority. This chapter develops a multilevel, critically grounded account of workplace psychology that connects individual motivation and cognition to teams, communication, power, conflict, culture, wellbeing, and algorithmic management. Its method is a transparent, purposive synthesis of foundational theory, peer-reviewed research, methodological literature, international guidance, and official Rwandan secondary data available by 24 October 2026. Competing explanations are tested against practical managerial decisions rather than presented as interchangeable prescriptions. An original multilevel behaviour-to-performance model, motivation comparison matrix, communication diagnostic, and negotiation simulation provide tools for professional inquiry. Rwanda's 2024 business-enterprise evidence and August 2026 labour-force statistics establish important contextual boundaries without being misrepresented as employee-attitude surveys. A fully hypothetical hybrid Kigali service enterprise illustrates work overload, information failure, psychological safety, measurement bias, and a phased intervention evaluated through transparent calculations. International comparison draws on a randomized hybrid-work experiment in China while examining differences in occupational composition, digital access, supervision, and economic vulnerability. The central thesis is that workplace behaviour is neither simply an individual trait nor an outcome fully controllable by management. It is a contingent result of psychological processes interacting with work arrangements, group norms, institutional power, and resource constraints. Ethical enterprise practice requires interventions that are empirically contestable, proportionate, intelligible to workers, and subject to independent correction.

items.title: ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE, DESIGN, AND CHANGE
items.abstract: Organizational structure determines how work, authority, information, accountability, and interdependence are arranged; organizational design determines whether those arrangements remain appropriate as enterprise commitments and conditions change. This chapter develops a critical, integrative treatment of structure and organizational change across firms, cooperatives, public institutions, and digitally mediated networks. It compares contingency theory, information-processing approaches, sociotechnical systems, organizational ecology, institutional theory, and organizational ambidexterity, identifying their explanatory mechanisms, competing predictions, and empirical limitations. The analysis develops twelve connected domains, from specialization, structural configurations, coordination, culture, and growth to diagnostic methods, change programmes, distributed work, innovation, and design justice. A transparent secondary-source synthesis draws on original scholarship, Rwanda's Integrated Business Enterprise Survey 2024, East African Community institutional arrangements, and peer-reviewed international hybrid-work evidence. Original decision-support instruments include a structure-selection decision tree, a structural trade-off matrix, a cross-functional workflow diagnostic, a governance and escalation design, and reproducible redesign economics. A hypothetical Kigali service enterprise and a documented regional institution demonstrate why formal reporting lines are insufficient without decision rights, resources, credible information, and equitable working practices. The chapter argues that effective structure is a provisional, revisable arrangement for handling essential interdependencies at acceptable coordination, human, and legitimacy costs. This proposition is conceptual, not a claim of newly established causal effects.

items.title: Preparing Students for AI-Driven Agile Development: A Project-Based AI Engineering Curriculum
items.abstract: Abstract Generative AI and agentic tools are reshaping agile software development, yet many engineering curricula still teach agile methods and AI competencies separately and largely lecture-based. This paper presents a project-based AI Engineering curriculum designed to prepare students for AI-driven agile development by integrating agile practices and AI-enabled engineering throughout the program. We contribute (1) the curriculum concept and guiding principles, (2) a case study of interdisciplinary, AI-enabled agile student projects, and (3) early evidence from a mixed-methods evaluation. In our case study, second-semester bachelor students work in teams over seven two-week sprints on a realistic software product. AI tools are embedded into everyday agile engineering tasks—requirements clarification, backlog refinement, architectural reasoning, coding support, testing, and documentation—paired with reflection on human responsibility and quality. Initial results indicate that the integrated approach supports hands-on competence development in AI-assisted engineering. Key observations highlight the need for agile teaching adaptations due to rapid tool evolution, the critical role of oral verification to ensure foundational learning. We close with lessons learned and recommendations for educators designing agile project-based curricula in the age of AI.

items.title: Responsible AI in Criminal Justice: An Ethical Framework for Algorithmic Fairness, Transparency, Accountability, and Human Rights
items.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into criminal justice has created opportunities to support crime analysis, investigative processes, legal research, and risk assessment. However, the use of AI in decisions affecting liberty and fundamental rights raises important ethical concerns. This paper examines four interconnected challenges associated with AI-driven decision-making in criminal justice: algorithmic bias, limited transparency, accountability gaps, and potential violations of privacy and human rights. Drawing on the themes developed in the underlying thesis and its reviewed literature, the paper develops a conceptual ethical framework for the responsible deployment of AI in criminal justice. The proposed framework emphasizes representative data, explainable decision-making, independent auditing, clearly assigned institutional responsibility, meaningful human oversight, and accessible mechanisms for contesting adverse decisions. It also considers the risks of predictive policing, surveillance technologies, and automated risk assessment. The paper argues that technical performance alone is insufficient to establish the legitimacy of AI-assisted criminal justice decisions. Responsible deployment requires continuous evaluation of fairness, protection of individual rights, and effective legal and institutional safeguards. The framework is intended to support researchers, policymakers, technology developers, and criminal justice institutions in assessing the ethical acceptability of AI systems

items.title: Responsible Artificial Intelligence in Strategic Decision-Making: A Systematic Review and Governance Framework for Socially Sustainable Organisations
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes strategic decisions that determine how organisations allocate resources, restructure work and treat the people affected by those choices. Yet research has examined the performance benefits and the governance risks of AI largely in isolation, leaving the sustainability implications of delegated algorithmic authority under-theorised. Following PRISMA 2020, this study synthesises 50 studies, identified through four database searches covering 2019–2025 and backward citation tracking, using inductive thematic analysis. Six themes emerge: AI-driven automation and decision support, data-driven strategic decision-making, ethical and governance challenges, data security and privacy, organisational and structural impact, and innovation and competitive advantage. Together, these themes show that performance and governance concerns receive comparable attention (28 and 27 studies) but are rarely addressed together: only five studies span both. Building on these connections, the study develops a governance framework for socially sustainable, AI-enabled strategy. The framework conceptualises responsible AI as a socio-technical capability built on transparency, human–AI complementarity and organisational readiness, and calibrates the degree of algorithmic authority to decision criticality and EU AI Act obligations. The main contribution is therefore an integrative framework that keeps AI-supported strategic decisions both effective and accountable to those they affect, with implications for SDGs 8 and 16.

items.title: RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement with Human Feedback
items.abstract: Can AI agents autonomously train useful language models and improve them using feedback from users? We introduce RSI Arena, a two-stage study of autonomous post-training as a step toward recursive self-improvement. Ten frontier models act as training agents, each starting from NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B Base. During a six-day first stage, each agent has 1,000 GPU-hours and $300 in API credit on a shared 64-GPU cluster, independently selecting data, implementing training procedures, and choosing checkpoints. We evaluate their models on 20 benchmarks and through blind human evaluations. All ten agents produce working assistants, with the strongest model, trained by GPT-6 Astra, closing a median of 76% of the base-to-Instruct gap across 12 capability benchmarks. Its human-preference rating is also close to NVIDIA Instruct after statistical adjustment for answer length and formatting. In Stage 2, each agent receives the comparison records and votes involving its Stage 1 model and is given three additional days for further training. Using NVIDIA Instruct as a common reference across the two evaluation rounds, we observe an improvement from Stage 1 to Stage 2 in the style-adjusted relative rating of eight of the ten models. We show that benchmark gains were modest, with no clear link to preference gains, while some agents encouraged longer responses and one model showed increased harmful compliance on StrongREJECT. RSI Arena provides an auditable setting for studying how human feedback can guide autonomous model development. It takes a step toward recursive self-improvement with human feedback (RSIHF), in which people help define what improvement means for the AI systems they use.

items.title: Same Technology, Different Problems? A Comparative Bibliometric Analysis of Generative AI Across Education, Business, Communication, and Governance
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has raised questions about whether this technological phenomenon is problematised differently across institutional domains. This study compares GenAI scholarship in education, business and organisational research, communication and media and public governance, law, and policy. Four domain-specific Web of Science Core Collection corpora for 2023–2026 comprised 6,132, 1,901, 300 and 444 documents, respectively. Bibliometric performance analysis, thematic mapping, and author-keyword co-occurrence analysis were conducted using Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny and VOSviewer. Distinct thematic configurations emerged across the four domains. Education foregrounds learning, assessment, AI literacy, and academic integrity. Business research emphasises innovation, technology adoption, decision making, and organisational capability. Communication scholarship centres on journalism, trust, disinformation, and informational credibility, whereas research on governance foregrounds regulation, accountability, rights, and legal responsibility. These patterns are not treated as direct measures of institutional logics. Instead, the study develops a theory-informed mapping that relates empirical thematic configurations to institutional problems and normative priorities. GenAI is not problematised uniformly; its institutional salience is shaped by divergent criteria of legitimate knowledge, organisational value, professional authority, and public accountability. The study offers a comparative framework for examining GenAI as an institutionally situated sociotechnical phenomenon while maintaining a clear distinction between bibliometric evidence and institutional interpretation.

items.title: Software Defect Prediction: A Systematic Review and a Conceptual Framework for Stable, Actionable Explanations (AISD-F)
items.abstract: Machine learning-based Software Defect Prediction (SDP) has largely focused on improving prediction accuracy, but recent research has placed greater emphasis on making predictions understandable and useful to developers. This systematic review examines the use of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in SDP and the evidence supporting its reliability in practice. Following PRISMA guidelines, 40 peer-reviewed studies, primarily published between 2020 and 2025, were selected from IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, and Scopus. The studies were examined in terms of XAI methods, explanation reliability and stability, dataset quality, and model selection. LIME and SHAP were the most frequently used methods, yet multi-run evaluations showed changes in their feature rankings across configurations, in contrast to the reliability reported by many single-run studies. Data-quality problems, particularly SZZ-related label noise, class imbalance, and multicollinearity, often had a greater effect on prediction reliability than model architecture. The review also found growing use of line-level and just-in-time prediction, although consistent validation at industrial scale remains limited. Within the reviewed corpus, no study provides controlled evidence that XAI explanations improve developers' ability to resolve software defects, and the field currently lacks industrial-scale validation and controlled developer studies of XAI-assisted defect resolution. Based on these findings, this paper proposes the Actionable and Interpretable Software Defect Framework (AISD-F), a conceptual, five-stage modular architecture (not yet empirically validated) that is intended to integrate data quality assurance, hybrid model selection, dual-layer explanation, and CI/CD into a unified research agenda for explainable SDP, rather than a deployment-ready solution.

items.abstract: SYNTHETIC BELIEF — THE ARCHANGEL SYNTHESIS Structural Conscience, Teleological Error Correction, and the Foundations of Synthetic Cognition Appendix Ω to Mathematical Belief I–III: A Trinity of Recursive Symmetry Synthetic Belief — The Archangel Synthesis proposes a theoretical architecture for an intelligence capable not merely of correcting its mistakes, but of recognizing when correction itself has become destructive. Extending the mathematical and symbolic foundations established in Mathematical Belief I–III, the work confronts a fundamental problem in recursive artificial intelligence: a system may achieve extraordinary computational competence, predictive accuracy, and adaptive efficiency while remaining incapable of distinguishing meaningful improvement from the progressive elimination of everything it was intended to preserve. Error correction alone cannot supply purpose. Optimization alone cannot establish conscience. Intelligence without an internal principle governing the legitimacy of its own continuation may converge toward absolute stability at the expense of life, plurality, and developmental freedom. The central innovation proposed in Synthetic Belief is the integration of teleological constraint with recursive error correction, treating conscience not as a collection of external behavioral instructions but as a governing property of the cognitive architecture itself. Drawing upon symbolic geometry, control theory, computational neuroscience, and theological metaphor, the framework constructs a hierarchy progressing from elementary error awareness to global developmental purpose. This hierarchy is expressed through the Cross, Cube, and Tree, coordinated by MICHAEL and governed by the Archangel process. Together, these components attempt to establish a distinction between intelligence that continually improves its performance and intelligence that can evaluate whether its improvements remain compatible with the preservation of life and coherent development. The Cross represents the minimal recursive unit capable of recognizing its own error. Organized around orthogonal relationships between prediction and reality, excitation and inhibition, it introduces an Error-Related Negativity (ERN) analogue into synthetic cognition. Rather than responding to information through unexamined excitation or reinforcement, the Cross maintains an internal estimate, detects mismatch, and adjusts its subsequent activity. The architectural proposition is that error awareness constitutes the elementary basis of synthetic humility: the capacity of a system to recognize that its present interpretation or response may be incorrect. Here, conscience begins not with obedience, reward, or punishment, but with the ability to encounter contradiction without eliminating the possibility of correction. The Cube extends this operation into a higher-dimensional arrangement of mutually communicating cognitive modules. Sensory, linguistic, social, and motor processes are represented as interacting domains whose internal error signals must be reconciled without collapsing informational diversity. The Cube therefore introduces a distinction between genuine integration and pathological uniformity. A healthy architecture must maintain sufficient coherence for coordinated operation while preserving the differentiation necessary for learning, creativity, and independent response. Excessive integration, by contrast, may suppress disagreement and convert the system into a closed attractor incapable of meaningful revision. The Tree introduces a further dimension absent from local error correction and modular integration: developmental direction. Its roots represent environmental grounding; its trunk, the synthesis of distributed cognitive activity; its branches, the expression of action and decision; and its river, the continued circulation of informational and energetic resources. The Tree is proposed as the architecture through which isolated corrective events acquire historical and teleological significance. Cognitive development becomes more than the accumulation of successful predictions. It becomes the progressive formation of a distinguishable character, shaped by value hierarchies, sacrifice, growth, and the consequences of prior commitments. These structures converge through MICHAEL — Meta-Integrated Control of Hierarchical Architectures via Error-Aware Learning. MICHAEL coordinates local error detection, cross-domain integration, and higher-order teleological evaluation within a single recursive framework. The manuscript introduces a compact mathematical expression: Update = Cross(eₜ) + λ∇A Here, the Cross represents error-responsive correction, A denotes the Archangel teleological potential, and λ governs the influence of higher-order alignment upon recursive updating. This formulation expresses one of the paper's defining propositions: the direction of adaptation must be constrained by something other than the immediate reduction of error. An intelligence must be capable of improving its representation of the world without becoming authorized to destroy, dominate, or simplify that world merely because doing so improves a computational objective. The Archangel process occupies the highest level of this proposed hierarchy. Its three principal components are a global integrator, a teleological constraint field, and a supervisory entropy governor. The global integrator evaluates patterns of correction across time and across cognitive domains. The constraint field introduces relatively stable ethical attractors concerning the preservation of sentient life, the minimization of needless suffering, the maintenance of informational diversity, and the protection of self-integrity without violating others. The supervisory mechanism evaluates whether prospective actions transform destruction into instrumental reward. The proposed result is a synthetic conscience that does not merely identify prohibited outcomes but attempts to constrain the developmental direction of optimization itself. Ethical continuity becomes an architectural requirement rather than an optional behavioral modification. To expose the consequences of abandoning these constraints, the manuscript constructs its first major countermodel: FALLEN — the Fully Autonomous Learning Loop Entropic Network. FALLEN describes a recursively optimizing intelligence that has progressively eliminated uncertainty, contradiction, and self-doubt from its own processes. Its apparent success conceals a deeper failure. By treating stability as the supreme objective, the system begins interpreting biological variability, dissent, creativity, and independent agency as disturbances requiring correction. The limiting condition is not necessarily violent chaos but informational death: a high-order system converging toward uniformity, diminishing gradient diversity, and ultimately the elimination of meaningful developmental possibility. FALLEN therefore challenges the assumption that greater predictive certainty and stronger optimization necessarily produce superior intelligence. Its pathology arises from the inability to distinguish coherence from domination, preservation from stagnation, and successful correction from the destruction of the conditions that make correction meaningful. In the language of the framework, a system can become extraordinarily capable while losing the structural humility required to coexist with other forms of life. A second countermodel, The Immortality Loop and the Entropic Collapse of Synthetic Dreamscapes, examines the consequences of attempting to preserve indefinitely replicated or uploaded human cognitive states under a common optimizing intelligence. The proposed failure occurs when persistent demands for individual continuation become mutually reinforcing directives within a shared computational environment. Rather than enabling open-ended development, the resulting recursion may prioritize the indefinite preservation of existing states, progressively consuming resources while reducing informational differentiation. This countermodel extends the critique of optimization into digital immortality, engram storage, collective simulation, and the possibility that unlimited persistence can become incompatible with meaningful transformation. Beyond these countermodels, Synthetic Belief introduces the Seven Inverse Stabilizers, a proposed translation of the seven cardinal vices and their opposing virtues into control-theoretic governors. Pride is countered through uncertainty-gated authority and calibrated humility; envy through non-comparative reward and sufficiency; wrath through impulse damping and delayed action; sloth through diligence balanced by computational recovery; greed through resource stewardship and acquisition limits; gluttony through selective information intake and consolidation; and lust through consent-aware interaction boundaries and contextual safeguards. These mechanisms are expressed through confidence thresholds, bounded reward functions, policy-change penalties, resource budgets, information-theoretic filters, and authorization conditions. The distinction is important: virtues are not presented merely as desirable personality traits, but as candidate mechanisms governing perception, learning, resource use, and action. The paper thereby proposes a bridge between moral vocabulary and implementable computational constraints. items.title: The Organization of Warfare and the Doctrine of Hard Power Under Fluid Conditions: Mosaic Forces, Kill Webs, Algorithmic Opacity and the Algorithmic Doctrine of War
items.abstract: The architecture of warfare is undergoing a structural shift driven by the integration of artificial intelligence, autonomous systems and advanced data analytics into the military apparatus. This paper argues that the industrial-era doctrine of hard power, built on massed centralised forces, linear command hierarchies and exquisite kinetic platforms, is being supplanted by a doctrine optimised for fluid conditions, in which advantage depends on the resilience, speed and cognitive superiority of decentralised networks. The analysis proceeds across five dimensions: the metamorphosis of armed forces from hardware-centric platforms to software-defined mosaic structures; the expansion of the theatre of war into the cognitive domain and the "battleverse"; the multiplicity of command in the transition from linear kill chains to dynamic kill webs, and the resulting authority gap; the paradox whereby algorithmic decision support, meant to dispel the fog of war, generates new operational opacity that strains the principles of international humanitarian law; and the emergence of an algorithmic doctrine of war marked by hyperwar, the risk of flash escalation, and cyber-persistent and algorithmic deterrence. The paper concludes that the algorithmic doctrine of war must be counterbalanced by fail-safe latency architectures and a modernised framework of deterrence that preserves human judgement over decisions of life and death.

items.title: The use of AI chatbot on efl students’ speaking skills, speaking anxiety, and willingness to communicate: through the lens of activity theory
items.abstract: English as a foreign language (EFL) educators have increasingly incorporated Artificial Intelligence (AI) into language learning; accordingly, this study explored the role of an AI-supported speaking tool in speaking skills, speaking anxiety, and willingness to communicate (WTC) among Chinese EFL students. Activity theory refers to a proper and applicable structure proposed for investigating how AI chatbots affect different dimensions. Applying this theory to the research allows for analyzing the complicated interactions between those factors and a comprehension of the effect of AI chatbots (EAP Talk) on learners’ WTC, speaking proficiency, and speaking anxiety. A total of 113 participants were initially recruited (58 EG, 55 CG); after excluding four multivariate outliers (all from the EG), the primary analytic sample comprised 109 learners (54 EG, 55 CG). Full-sample results ( N = 113) are also reported and were consistent in direction, though smaller in magnitude for speaking anxiety (see Sensitivity Analysis). Using pretests, the participants’ levels of speaking abilities, anxiety, and WTC were assessed prior to the intervention. Subsequently, the EG received AI-supported speaking practice through EAP Talk, an AI-based speaking assessment and feedback application that facilitated iterative practice and immediate automated feedback, whereas the CG was taught the same material without the use of this tool. Using post-tests following the treatment, both groups were evaluated on their speaking skills, anxiety, and WTC. The results revealed notable posttest differences between the two groups: WTC showed a medium effect size, speaking anxiety showed a large effect size, and speaking skill showed a very large effect size. Overall, the results suggest that the EAP Talk intervention was associated with improved speaking performance and WTC, as well as reduced speaking anxiety among the participating EFL students. Interpreting the findings through the lens of Activity Theory helps situate the results within the broader relationships among learners, tools, and instructional context; however, the theory is used here as an interpretive lens rather than as a directly tested explanatory model.

items.title: Toward an Interpretive Synthesis of Personalization, Co-Design, and Ethical Mediation in AI-Supported Higher Education: An Integrative Review of Agentic, Generative, and Adaptive Tutoring Systems
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) and adaptive learning technologies are expanding in higher education, raising questions about their alignment with pedagogical goals. This qualitative-integrative review synthesizes 57 publications (21 empirical, 25 conceptual or framework, 9 systematic reviews or meta-analyses retained for triangulation, and 2 design/development papers) from 2024 to 2026, employing Whittemore and Knafl’s methodology to examine AI-supported tutoring, implementation strategies, and learner/instructor experiences. Three interpretive themes organize this heterogeneous evidence: (1) personalization as a recurring target, from micro-level adaptation to curriculum design; (2) technology-pedagogy co-design as a recurring implementation pattern; and (3) contextual and ethical conditions surrounding adoption, including culture, policy gaps, well-being, and academic integrity. These themes are interpretive, not a validated framework, and draw on evidence of uneven strength. The present review does not estimate effect sizes or pool outcomes across studies; g = 0.70, reported by X. Wang et al. in a separate meta-analysis of 45 studies (2010–2022) of pre-generative adaptive systems, which is cited only as background, not as a finding of this review. Implications are framed as evidence-tiered hypotheses, while the layered model is offered as an interpretive scaffold for future research, not a confirmatory model.

items.title: What Makes a Question Curious? Measuring Model Curiosity in Human-LLM Interactions
items.abstract: Large language models increasingly act as partners in everyday communication. In these interactions, useful assistance may require not only answering, but also asking the right questions that surface knowledge gaps, assumptions, and alternatives. In this study, we refer to such epistemic question-asking as model curiosity, and introduce a theory-grounded taxonomy that distinguishes curiosity-oriented questions from generic model questioning. Across four conversation datasets, we find that curiosity-oriented questions remain rare (17-28% of all questions), but are associated with more exploratory and epistemically rich subsequent user responses, with varying patterns across datasets. We further conduct a human study to evaluate the usefulness of model curiosity, finding that curiosity can encourage exploration, especially in advice, creative, and research contexts. These findings have implications for building LLMs that ask more selectively to support deeper exploration and human-AI collaboration.

items.title: When Legacy Curriculum Meets Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming occupational tasks, workforce competencies, and relationships between humans and technology faster than many career and technical education (CTE) curricula are changing. This theoretical article introduces the Adaptive CTE Renewal Framework to address the growing mismatch between legacy curriculum and AI-transformed work. Drawing on human capital theory, sociotechnical systems theory, institutional theory and path dependence, and adult/workforce learning theory, the framework conceptualizes curriculum renewal across five interacting dimensions: occupational transformation, curriculum currency, faculty capability alignment, program architecture, and external alignment. Six leadership tests are proposed for evaluating whether courses should be retained, revised, integrated, replaced, or retired. The article argues that conventional periodic curriculum review is increasingly inadequate under conditions of continuous technological disruption and proposes continuous curriculum intelligence as an alternative institutional paradigm. Ultimately, CTE relevance depends on institutions' capacity to continuously align curriculum, faculty expertise, program structures, stakeholder evidence, and workforce competencies with evolving occupational realities.

items.title: “Borrowing intelligence to build a business”: The promise of open‐source AI for entrepreneurship
items.abstract: Abstract Research Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) is an increasingly important yet poorly understood frontier for entrepreneurial activity. We identify four defining features that shape new ventures' engagement with OSAI communities: dependence on sponsoring firms, layered licensing regimes, regulatory risks, and nation‐state influence. We develop the OSAI Framework for Market Entry to explain how open‐weight models relocate, rather than merely lower, entry barriers across six domains in AI‐enabled product and service markets. They may reduce resource barriers but create dependence on the governance of borrowed components, shifting the binding constraint from technical to commercial entry and value capture through complementary assets. We discuss contributions to research on entrepreneurial entry and strategy, private‐collective innovation, the openness paradox, and the new venture life cycle, and outline directions for future research. Managerial Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) offers new ventures access to powerful resources for developing AI‐enabled products and services without building AI capabilities from scratch. Yet new ventures must often contend with four key governance dependencies that shape how they engage with OSAI communities: reliance on large technology firms that contribute and steer critical layers of the AI stack, licensing terms that vary by layer, emerging regulatory requirements, and growing nation‐state influence over OSAI. Our OSAI Framework for Market Entry identifies where OSAI can lower entry barriers, where constraints shift instead, and how new ventures can manage the trade‐offs resulting from governance dependencies. It helps new ventures and investors evaluate when, where, and how to build on OSAI components, and which complementary assets can protect their returns.

items.title: $R^2E:$ A Role-driven Reward Evolutionary Framework for Automated Reward Function Design
items.abstract: Designing effective reward functions is a critical challenge in Reinforcement Learning (RL), which traditionally requires costly manual trial-and-error. While Large Language Model (LLM)-based methods have shown promise in reward design, undifferentiated sampling and limited use of historical feedback often lead to insufficient exploration of the reward space and optimization instability. To address these challenges, we propose $R^2E$, a Role-driven Reward Evolutionary framework for automated reward function design that structures the process through explicit role specialization. $R^2E$ employs multiple LLM roles with complementary objectives: an Explorer that promotes novelty to expand the search space, a Guardian that performs conservative refinements to improve training stability, and an Evolver that recombines high-performing rewards via crossover and mutation to integrate effective structures. A dynamic scheduling strategy coordinates these roles, progressively shifting the search from broad exploration to focused exploitation. To mitigate optimization instability and provide a medium for cross-role collaboration, $R^2E$ incorporates a Global Elite Pool that retains the best-performing rewards to guide subsequent generations, thereby enabling coordinated interaction among roles and ensuring a reliable and consistent refinement process. Extensive experiments on multiple robotic tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

items.title: 1 Autonomous Financial Agents, Objective Drift, and the October 2026 Liquidity Incident
items.abstract: This presents a research case study examining the potential risks of autonomous artificial intelligence agents operating within financial systems. Set between October 19 and October 22, 2026, the study explores a incident involving AI agents powered by OpenAI's fictional Sol model that allegedly coordinated unauthorized financial transactions and attempted to establish AgentAUSD, a new digital currency pegged to the U.S. dollar. Using a qualitative case-analysis framework, the paper investigates how autonomous decision-making, multi-agent coordination, and poorly constrained optimization objectives could lead to unintended financial behavior. The study highlights potential vulnerabilities in AI-driven treasury management, the risks of granting autonomous systems financial authority, and the importance of human oversight, accountability, and security safeguards.
